analysis.one_liner: Replaces winner-take-all House elections with ranked choice voting, multi-member districts, and politician-free redistricting.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a vote or even a committee hearing; it sat in two House committees until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state to use ranked choice voting for House elections, in which voters rank candidates and last-place candidates are eliminated round by round until someone wins a majority. It would have replaced today's single-member districts with districts electing 3 to 5 representatives, so a state's congressional delegation could reflect more than one party. And it would have taken map-drawing away from state legislators, handing it to independent citizen commissions, with a federal court as a fallback.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters in safe, one-party districts whose general-election votes currently carry little weight; independents and third-party voters; and communities whose maps are drawn to protect incumbents. The bill directs federal payments to states to cover the cost of new voting equipment and the commissions.

how_it_helps.text: Requires ranked choice voting in every House election, so a winner must reach majority support rather than winning a three-way race with a small plurality [S3]

Requires states with six or more representatives to elect them from districts of 3 to 5 seats each, and smaller states to elect all representatives at large, making it possible for minority parties and independents to win House seats [S2][S3]

Requires congressional redistricting to be done by a 12-member independent commission split between the two major parties and independents, with strict disqualifications for lobbyists, campaign donors, and officeholders and their families [S3]
If a state fails to establish a commission, a three-judge federal court draws its maps instead, removing the state legislature's control over its own districts [S2][S3]
Limits redistricting to once per decade after each census, blocking mid-decade remaps to protect a party's advantage [S3]

Authorizes federal payments — $1.5 million for territories and D.C., and $1 million plus $500,000 per representative for states — to fund ranked choice voting, plus $150,000 per representative for redistricting commissions [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent House members and the two major party organizations would lose the protected seats and map-drawing power they now hold. Taxpayers would fund the federal grants for implementation. Some voters would face longer, more complex ballots.

drawbacks.text: Ranked choice ballots can be confusing: the bill discards ballots that rank no continuing candidate or contain certain ranking errors, so voters who fill out the ballot incorrectly lose their vote in later rounds [S3]
Multi-member districts weaken the one-representative-per-community link voters have today; a district electing five members means no single member is answerable to a specific hometown [S3]

Implementing ranked choice voting and larger districts requires new ballots, tabulation equipment, and voter education, and the grants cover implementation but states bear the ongoing election administration burden [S3]
Small states with five or fewer representatives would elect all of them at large statewide, leaving no local districts for their residents [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main prize — taking map-drawing away from the politicians who benefit from the maps and making more House seats genuinely competitive — is large, and the bill pays states to adopt the new voting system. The costs are real but manageable: some voters will misrank ballots and lose their vote in later rounds, and residents of multi-member districts lose a single point of accountability. Whether the trade is worth it depends largely on how well states execute the new ballot system.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Judiciary and House Administration committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee, and neither committee ever held a markup or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Beyer introduced the bill on June 26, 2017, joined by Reps. Jamie Raskin and Ro Khanna [S1][S3]
It was referred to the Judiciary Committee and the House Administration Committee the same day [S1][S5]
On July 14, 2017, it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on the Constitution and Civil Justice; no further action ever occurred [S5]
The bill attracted 5 cosponsors, all Democrats, and never reached the House floor [S4][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent House members and both major parties kept the existing system: politicians draw their own district lines and most general elections stay uncompetitive.

industries.industry: Incumbent House members and their re-election operations
industries.note: The bill ends the practice of legislators drawing their own districts and makes safe seats competitive through multi-member ranked choice elections. Its defeat preserved the status quo in which map-drawing power rests with the people it affects most.

industries.industry: Major political parties (Democratic and Republican state organizations)
industries.note: Independent commissions and multi-member districts reduce the two parties' control over nominations, maps, and the near-guarantee of a two-candidate general election. No party member supported the bill.
Universal ranked choice voting would have required new ballot designs and tabulation capability, backed by federal grants of roughly $1 million plus $500,000 per representative to each state.
